## Six agent systems, one person signing off
I run a personal multi-agent platform on open-source Hermes Agent. I did not write Hermes. My part is the design: which agent owns what, how work moves between them, and where it has to stop for me.
A router and 10 domain agents each own one area. Work moves on kanban cards, from an orchestrator to a worker and then to a review gate.
Running since 11 Sep 2026, on a cloud server since 20 Sep 2026. Build log

# Multi-agent platform
Source: https://krishnendu.me/work/platform/

## Multi agent operations platform: 11 agents, one job each, and my approval on risky steps
The platform runs on Hermes Agent, an open source agent runtime from Nous Research. The design is mine: which agent owns what, how work is handed between them, and where it stops for me. Private system; architecture and verified telemetry shown here.
Agents
11 agents
1 router + 10 domain agents
Recurring Jobs
52 recurring jobs
53 enabled including one offs, counted 10 Oct 2026
Logged Hours
179.8 h
logged with the agents over 24 active days
Human Gate
Human gate
sends, deletes and public pushes wait for me
## Why eleven agents and not one
One agent that does everything carries every instruction at once and holds every key at once. The agent drafting an email does not need deployment credentials; the agent parsing receipts does not need my LinkedIn drafts. Mixed instructions produce mixed behaviour, and shared access turns one mistake into a wide one.
So the work is partitioned the way a company partitions departments: mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive. Each agent has one domain, its own workspace, its own memory, and only the tools that domain needs. A router decides who owns a request. A medic checks hourly that nobody has drifted out of lane.
## Topology
Eleven agents, one owner per domain, no overlap. Alongside the 11 agents, a typed decision model answers narrow questions for them; details on Fast decisions .
Who owns what: one router, ten domain agents, one gate. Dashed lines are audit and planning paths, not request paths.
Component Role Permissions and Policy
Me Dictate, check, send Reviews risky steps
Hermes Gateway Ingestion Discord and Telegram gateways
Router (default) Central dispatcher Classifies intent, assigns task cards
Kanban Board Coordination Task card hand offs, parent child tasks

Finance Receipts and accounting Rule based parsing to Firefly III

9Router Model gateway Model routing and fallback
## Router
The default agent receives every message from Discord or Telegram, classifies it, and hands it to the owning domain agent as a kanban card. It does small lookups itself only when routing would cost more than the task.
## Domain agents
Academics: Coursework at IIM Ranchi and IIT Madras, research reading and deadlines.
Career prep: My own applications, resume and interview prep.
Finance: Receipts to ledger, self hosted Firefly III.
Infrastructure: Declared system state, services, backups, secrets.
Personal ops: Tasks, briefings, reminders, habits.
Socials: LinkedIn and personal posts, drafted by the agent, published by me.
Consulting: Commercial go to market consulting.
Medic: Hourly audit of estate structure and health, reports to a status channel.
Janitor: Finds disk clutter, proposes deletions, acts only on my approval.
Private: One agent for institute work, not described here.
## Kanban hand offs
Work moves as cards: objective, context, acceptance criteria, owner. The router writes the card, the owner session writes the artifact, and a card can spawn read only children for research or critique. Cross domain jobs are separate cards linked by a parent, never one mixed artifact.
## Planning at maximum effort
Some tasks need a specification before anyone writes code: multi file architecture, design direction, fact audits. Those go to a planning pass I call Fable: the strongest available model at its highest reasoning tier, asked for an executable plan. Builders then follow the plan.
## Upkeep
A medic agent audits configuration drift every hour and files findings rather than silently fixing them. A janitor agent batches cleanup proposals and waits for my approval before deleting anything.
## How a request moves
I dictate, check the text, then send it. What needs me lands in Google Tasks.
How a request moves: read only steps happen before the gate. Risky steps wait for approval.
Step Stage Actor Action Gating
1 Input Me Dictate and check transcript Self review
2 Ingestion Gateway Deliver message via Discord or Telegram Automated
3 Triage Router Classify intent and write kanban card Automated
4 Dispatch Kanban Route card to domain agent Automated
5 Execution Domain agent Read only work: research, drafts, diffs Automated
6 Review Me Inspect diff or artifact at the human gate Approval required
7 Apply Domain agent Apply change and close task card Gated
8 Sync Google Tasks Sync open actionables that need me Automated
## Input
I dictate with FreeFlow on Mac or Dictate on Android, both free and open source, read the transcript, and send it as text on Discord or Telegram. I skip the runtime's own voice plugins on purpose: I want to see what got written before an agent acts on it.
## The gate
Anything I would regret waits for my approval: sends, deletes and public pushes. Outbound email, file deletion and public git pushes stop at the gate until I have inspected the diff or the artifact. A question to me has no timeout. An unanswered card parks; it does not proceed.
## Output
Important actionables that need me are synced to Google Tasks by an idempotent ledger, and a watcher logs what I complete or edit so the agents learn what I actually did.

About 6 agent replies for every message I send. That ratio is the point of the design: I write instructions, not code.
## How replies are counted
Assistant messages across every agent conversation database, including scheduled jobs and subagents, counted once each after removing copies created when long conversations are compacted (same role, timestamp and opening text). Tool results and my own messages are counted separately.
## Access from any device
I can run the whole platform from my phone, so work continues when my laptop is closed or not with me. Three pieces make that work.
Private mesh: Tailscale, a WireGuard based private network, joins three devices: the server (an Azure VPS, Linux), my MacBook Pro (macOS) and my phone (Android). I reach the server over the mesh, from those three devices.
Termius: I sometimes SSH in via Termius from my phone or laptop over Tailscale. It connects over the mesh, so I can check a service or restart one from the phone.
Dictation: I dictate on my phone or Mac (Dictate on Android, FreeFlow on Mac), read the transcript, then send it on Discord or Telegram. The router agent picks it up from there.
Access path to the Azure server: devices reach the server over the private mesh.
Device Tools Destination
Phone Termius, Dictate Azure VPS via Tailscale mesh
Laptop SSH, FreeFlow Azure VPS via Tailscale mesh
## Host, isolation and secrets
Every agent runs on one rented cloud server and stays inside its own workspace. The host is an Azure VPS running Ubuntu 24.04, and the runtime moved there from a MacBook Linux VM on 20 Sep 2026, so the agents run around the clock.
systemd services: Each long running piece, such as the model gateway and the chat gateway, runs as a system service that restarts on its own after a reboot.
Workspace isolation: Each agent has its own working directory, persistent memory, scoped tools and skills. Each domain keeps its own data in its own workspace.
## Secrets and backups
Secrets live in locked down files and a credential vault that fills only at its own origin; nothing secret is ever pasted into chat. Guard scripts check the context files each agent reads. State is backed up hourly, encrypted capsules go offsite daily to GitHub Releases, the offsite copy is verified weekly, and a scripted restore to a fresh server exists.
## What the review step has taught me
This page is built through the same pipeline: a planning card at maximum effort, a builder agent in the consulting profile, and a review gate before release. The review step is how stale figures on this very page were found: counts had been typed into prose and the system had moved on. The rebuild binds every number to the data file the agents maintain, so the gate now checks a script, not a memory.
Hermes Agent · Python · systemd · 9Router · Discord · Telegram · SQLite


# Model routing
Source: https://krishnendu.me/work/routing/

## Model routing and tiered compute: local gateway with fallback resilience
One gateway on my server in front of several model accounts, with backup models when one fails, and three effort levels for different kinds of work. Plain scripts handle deterministic computation before any model is invoked. Narrow yes or no and pick-one questions skip this table entirely; they go to my fast decision model .
Gateway
9Router gateway on my server
Routing Strategy
Backup models · 3 main effort levels (medium, high, max)
Core Invariant
Plain scripts run before any AI model
## Problem
Directly binding agent workflows to a single AI provider causes brittle failures when rate limits or upstream outages occur. Furthermore, sending basic data extraction or mechanical formatting tasks to expensive models wastes tokens and increases latency.
## What I Built
9Router gateway: A small service on my server that sits between most agents and the AI providers and moves a request to a backup model when one fails. Claude models are called directly.
Fable, my maximum effort tier: When a task needs multi-file planning, design direction or a deep fact audit, it is sent there to produce a specification before any code is written.
Deterministic First Rule: Exact computations (mathematical formulas, file system queries, regex extractions) must execute in native Python or Bash before passing structured context to an LLM.
## How the Gateway Pools Models
9Router pooling: 9Router runs on the server itself and gives most agents one address for many models. Behind it sits a pool of providers; if one provider rate-limits or fails, the request moves to the next one, with Gemini Flash as the default backup.
Cost tiering: Cheap, fast models take bulk work; the expensive model is reserved for steps where an error is costly. Plain scripts run first, so many tasks never reach a model. Cost figures are on the token ledger .
## Dynamic Routing and Complexity Tiering
Tasks are routed dynamically across models based on task complexity, speed, and cost efficiency: Gemini Flash handles high-volume sweeps and lightweight tools, Claude Sonnet handles deterministic code generation and test suites, and Claude Opus handles deep multi-file reasoning and architectural verification.
Gemini Flash: High-throughput sweeps, reading, scraping, telemetry, and lightweight tool handling.
Claude Sonnet: Deterministic code generation, test suites, refactoring, and generator scripts.
Claude Opus: Deep multi-file reasoning, verification gates, and quality audits.
Fable: Architectural planning, design system direction, and exhaustive fact audits.
Measured share of logged tokens: Gemini Flash 69.0%, Claude Opus 22.0%, Claude Sonnet 8.7%. Full table on the token ledger .
## How I keep model calls rare and cheap
Large model calls are the most expensive operation in an agent platform. I use an ordered ladder of six techniques so that only tasks requiring deep reasoning reach larger models:
Scripts first: 48 of 53 enabled scheduled jobs run as plain Python or Bash code with zero AI model calls. Exact mathematical sums, ledger arithmetic, and system health checks execute in native code.
Typed decisions: Narrow categorical choices, relevance checks, and 0-to-1 scoring route to a fast decision model that answers in ~300 ms for fractions of a cent. Details are on Fast decisions .
Smallest capable chat model: When a task requires natural language or tool use, it goes to the lowest tier capable of handling it (Gemini Flash for high-volume sweeps and lightweight tools, Claude Sonnet for deterministic code and tests, Claude Opus for deep multi-file reasoning). See the tier table above.
Prompt caching: Repeated tool definitions, system prompts, and repository context are served from cache (88.8% cache hit rate across prompt tokens). Full accounting is on the Token ledger .
Context compression: Long conversations are compacted into structured summary nodes by a cheaper model (55 sessions compressed so far), keeping history searchable without sending full raw transcripts. Details are on Memory .
Planner last: The top tier (Fable) is invoked only for high-leverage architectural planning, design direction, and exhaustive fact audits before writing code.
No dollar reductions or token counts avoided are claimed here; these rungs show the technical architecture that keeps large model calls rare.
## Outcome
When a provider hits a rate limit, work moves to a backup model instead of stopping. Plain scripts do the bulk filtering on the server, so the models get less to read and the numbers come out the same every time.
## Limits
Switching to a backup model can make a reply slower, so each call needs a sensible time limit.
## Stack
9Router · Python · Bash · REST APIs · Linux


# Fast decisions
Source: https://krishnendu.me/work/fast-decisions/

## Fast decisions: a small model so the large ones stay quiet
Most choices my agents make are narrow: is this headline relevant, which category is this email, is this note a lasting preference. I send those to a typed decision model called Jev instead of a large chat model. It answers with a choice or a score in about a third of a second.
System 1 vs System 2: System 1 is fast, cheap judgment that answers one narrow question in under a second; System 2 is slow, expensive reasoning that I save for work that needs it.
## What this layer does
The typed decision model returns one of two typed answers: a choice among options I list, or a calibrated score between 0 and 1. It does not write text and it does not chat. If it cannot answer, the call falls back to its previous route, so no decision is lost.

Handed to fallback route 84 (0.07%)
Score calls / choice calls 66,710 / 48,594
Fallback means the typed model did not return a usable verdict and the call site used its backup route. It measures availability, not correctness. I do not have a labelled truth set for these decisions, so I do not report an accuracy figure for my own data.
## What it replaced
Status Call sites
Previously an AI model call 18
Previously a fixed rule 4
Total live call sites 22
Candidates under review 4
Rejected after review 1
A call site is one place in my code that asks for a decision. One site can ask more than one type of question. These are counts of call sites, not measured before-and-after savings.
## Where the decisions come from
Decision family Decisions Share Previous route
A private work workflow 89,166 77% Chat model call
Research headline relevance 25,891 22% Chat model call
Everything else (memory curation, email category, next action, model tier choice) 247 0.2% Chat model call or fixed rule
About three quarters of all decisions come from one private workflow in my work. I report its volume and nothing else about it.
## What it costs
On a measured sample of 8,472 calls since 7 Oct 2026, the typed decision layer processed 4,999,067 input tokens and 938,948 output tokens (5,938,015 total tokens, about 701 tokens per call) and cost $0.2100, an average of about $0.0598 per day.
Output tokens are free on this service; list price was $0.042 per million input tokens.
Earlier verdicts in the log are not metered for tokens. Because I do not record the tokens a chat model would have used for each decision, I do not publish an estimated reduction figure. The measured fact is narrower: 115,304 decisions were handled by this layer instead of calling a chat model.
## Where I never use it
A typed model is probabilistic, so I exclude it by file from anything irreversible or trust critical. It never decides:
Sending email or messages
Deleting files or approving cleanup
Anything touching money, finance or payments
Secrets, credentials and vaults
Lists of people who asked not to be contacted
These paths stay deterministic plain code or wait for my explicit approval. The exclusion list is checked by the same registry that manages live sites.
## Limits
The typed decision model is not free of mistakes. On public classification datasets, a third party measured this model at 76 to 95 depending on the dataset, against 77 to 96 for a large chat model and 88 to 91 for a fine-tuned small classifier. Those benchmarks come from public datasets and are not my data; I treat them as an external reference, not a result on my workflows.
In my own use, 0.07% of calls returned no usable answer and went to the backup route. It answers only the narrow, typed questions I configure; it cannot reason through anything open-ended or explain why it reached a decision.
The current service runs on limited credit, so I am testing a free and local typed decision model to take over the same role. This page describes an architectural role rather than a permanent vendor.
Decisions that matter stay deterministic or come to me because a cheap wrong answer that cannot be undone is not cheap.
How typed decisions fit into my broader cost strategy is documented in the savings ladder on Model routing and tiered compute
## Method note
Decision counts, latency percentiles, fallback counts, and call site numbers are read from the verdict log and decision registry at build time and refreshed every 6 hours. Test rows (identifiers starting with smoke, test, or probe) are excluded before counting. Times are wall-clock per call as logged by my client, including network latency. Fallback measures availability when the model returned no usable answer, not correctness against ground truth. Token and spend counts are from the meter started on 7 Oct 2026 (8,472 calls); earlier calls were not token-metered. Jev runs through its own service rather than the model gateway, so none of these calls appear in the Token ledger.


# How my agents remember: five layers of memory I can read and edit
Source: https://krishnendu.me/work/memory/

## How my agents remember: five layers of memory I can read and edit
How 11 agents on one Azure server remember what matters across months of daily work. Small notes I can read and edit keep the active rules fresh, while full searchable history on my own server preserves every past conversation.
The Core Difference: Hosted AI memory lives on a provider's servers in its format; I can view or delete entries but not version, script or move the files. Mine is split into five layers I own. What must survive permanently sits in plain Markdown files with strict character caps, so I can open, audit and edit them in seconds with any text editor. Past conversation history is kept in a local SQLite database on my own server (LCM-X), allowing agents to search earlier turns without crowding their active working window.
Production platform
Hermes Agent on Azure VPS · SQLite WAL · Markdown
Design principle
Short curated files for permanent rules · Searchable database for history
Human oversight
Agent operations run with human approval gates for irreversible actions
5 Memory layers
11 Agents
2,200 Char cap on notes
301,985 Messages in history
## Architecture: the five layer hierarchy
Each layer has one specific job, one retention rule, one size budget, and one gate on who may write to it. The model reads only L1 directly. Everything else arrives through the context assembler or a tool call.
Diagram A. Five layer memory architecture. Only L1 is read directly by the model. L3 and L4 load in full, L5 skills load on demand when a task matches, and older history is compacted into lcm.db for search and recall.
## The problem: remembering everything makes agents worse
Agents that try to remember everything fail in two quiet ways. The context window fills with stale detail, so the model spends attention on noise. And a store full of unchecked fragments lets the model recall things that were never true. Neither failure raises a clean error.
Cutting old messages blindly is not the answer either: the agent forgets earlier decisions, and a retried task starts from zero. I wanted durable memory small enough to read and audit in full, every durable write reversible, and the bulk of history compressed for the model without ever being thrown away.
## How the five layers work
L1 Session window and system prompt: The live working desk. Holds the system prompt, the agent's role rules, active conversation turns, and tool results. When it grows past the compaction threshold, LCM-X folds the oldest turns into summary nodes and preserves pointers to the original messages.
L2 Ephemeral scratch: The scratchpad. Each agent's TMPDIR points to its own cache/scratch directory. Downloads, extracted archives, and probe scripts land here. Nothing in scratch is read by subsequent sessions, and entries idle for 24 hours are pruned automatically.
L3 Curated persistent memory: The personal notebook. Two plain Markdown files per agent, MEMORY.md for system notes and USER.md for my profile, with hard character caps (2,200 and 2,600 characters on the router agent). Both files are loaded in full into every session, eliminating vector ranking latency and missed context. The strict cap forces active curation.
L4 Curated knowledge base: The reference library. 16 Markdown files in ~/.hermes/knowledge, organized with one topic per file. Contains verified facts about me, systems, and operating boundaries, edited by hand and read on demand per domain.
L5 Procedural skills library: The workshop tool rack. 347 SKILL.md files (235 distinct skills) across the router and 10 domain agents. Each skill defines activation triggers, step-by-step procedures, exit criteria, and runnable scripts. Skills represent executable procedures rather than raw facts, keeping them separate from L4.
## Layer specifications
Memory layer specifications

## Curation, human approval gates, and rollback
Writes to persistent memory (L3) never go straight to disk. They pass through a structured validation pipeline with snapshots, so any incorrect fact can be rolled back instantly.
Pending queue: Proposed memory writes requiring review are saved as JSON records in ~/.hermes/pending/memory rather than applied directly.
Pre-filter: A fast gate checks candidate writes to discard transient session noise before deeper evaluation.
Review tier: Fable, the top reasoning tier, evaluates each candidate. Durable operational facts and user preferences are accepted. Routine task progress is logged only, since LCM-X already records full transcripts. Irreversible changes (such as deletions, security boundaries, or suppression lists) wait for my manual confirmation.
Snapshot backup: Before modifying memory, the curator copies MEMORY.md and USER.md to timestamped files in memories/backups (3 snapshots on disk today).
Atomic apply: Approved updates use atomic file operations (write to temporary file, fsync, and rename) behind file locks, ensuring no agent ever reads a partially written file. The memory tool strictly rejects updates exceeding the character limit until old entries are consolidated.
Audit ledger and recovery: A local SQLite ledger tracks the source session and reasoning behind every remembered fact. If an incorrect claim is detected, restoring the previous snapshot takes one command. Explicit forgetting leaves a clean audit tombstone.
In addition, an automated hourly job backs up agent state and memory files, and a daily guard script checks that knowledge edits stay within their assigned topic files.
## LCM-X: lossless context memory
LCM-X operates beneath L1. Every message sent or received is recorded once in lcm.db with an immutable store_id. When the active context window fills up, LCM-X compacts older messages into a depth 0 summary node that references the exact store_ids it summarizes. When multiple depth 0 nodes accumulate, they compact into a depth 1 node. This creates a clean directed acyclic graph where summaries always link back to the exact source messages, and compaction never deletes or alters raw history.
Diagram B. Compaction shortens what the model reads, not what the store keeps. Every summary node lists the ids it covers, so a search can land on any level and lcm_expand can return the original text. Bottom figures are probed from the router agent's lcm.db at build time.
Compaction: The router agent's database currently holds 301,985 messages from 186 sessions and 64 summary nodes (62 at depth 0, 2 at depth 1). Maximum depth currently in use: 1.
FTS5 search: SQLite FTS5 full-text indexing indexes all messages and summary nodes. Search ranks results by keyword match strength and recency, allowing agents to pinpoint exact filenames, error strings, and identifiers instantly.
Lossless expansion: If an agent needs full historical context beyond a summary, the lcm_expand tool fetches the exact source messages by store_id or node_id. Compaction reduces token load in the active prompt without losing historical fidelity.
Concurrent WAL mode: SQLite Write-Ahead Logging allows background compaction jobs to write without blocking active agent reads.

Integrity check for the lossless DAG claim: every store_id and node_id referenced in a summary node must exist in the database. Result on 10 Oct 2026: 0 dangling references out of 4,377.
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM summary_nodes s, json_each(s.source_ids) j
WHERE (s.source_type = 'messages'
AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM messages m WHERE m.store_id = j.value))
OR (s.source_type <> 'messages'
AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM summary_nodes n WHERE n.node_id = j.value));
## Prototype vs production lineage
## Prototyping history
From 11 to 20 Sep 2026, the initial platform prototype ran in a local Linux virtual machine on my MacBook, testing local vector embeddings and the Hindsight memory API. On 20 Sep 2026, the platform migrated to an Azure Linux server. Hindsight and local embeddings were retired and never deployed to production. Production memory uses the five structured layers described above, powered by native Markdown curation and LCM-X on SQLite.
Prototype compared with production
Attribute Laptop prototype (11 to 20 Sep 2026) Azure VPS production (Current)
Historical recall Local vector embeddings LCM-X on SQLite WAL with FTS5 keyword indexing
Persistent memory Hindsight API Curated Markdown files with strict character caps
Deployment status Retired prototype, never deployed to VPS Active production system
## Key design decisions
Hard character caps over soft limits: Soft warnings get ignored during complex tasks. Hard limits force active consolidation before new facts are saved.
Plain Markdown over key-value databases: Human-readable, diffable, and directly editable with any standard text editor.
SQLite WAL over append-only JSONL files: Transactional safety, non-blocking concurrent reads, and built-in FTS5 search in a single file.
Exact keyword search over vector embeddings: Most developer and agent lookups require exact file paths, error codes, and entity names, where keyword search provides zero-hallucination precision.
Preserving raw evidence: Summaries represent compact interpretations. The underlying source messages remain the ground truth evidence.
## Failure modes and automated recovery
Failure modes and recovery
Failure condition Detection mechanism Automated recovery path
Write exceeds L3 character cap Memory tool enforces hard boundary Rejects write and prompts consolidation
Incorrect fact added to memory Curator audit and ledger tracking Restore previous snapshot or mark with tombstone
Summary lacks needed detail Summary lists covered store_ids lcm_expand retrieves full original turns
Dangling reference in summary DAG Automated integrity build query Page reports count; builds flag inconsistencies
Knowledge file drift Daily md_guard.py scan Alerts on misplaced content across topic files

See how memory connects with the rest of the multi-agent operations platform
## Stack
Hermes Agent · LCM-X · SQLite WAL · FTS5 · Python · Markdown


# Reliability and security
Source: https://krishnendu.me/work/reliability/

## Reliability and security: encrypted backup capsules and locked-down secrets
Encrypted nightly backups copied offsite to cloud storage and a private GitHub repository, locked-down secrets, and a scripted rebuild on a fresh server.
Timers
hermes-backup · hermes-offsite · hermes-offsite-verify · hermes-capsule-drift
Offsite Target
Encrypted offsite copies (cloud storage plus a private GitHub mirror)
Secrets Isolation
Locked-down secret files · a password vault that only fills the matching website
## Problem
Agents that can run commands on a server can leak keys, slowly change settings by accident, or lose work when the server restarts. Reliable operations require continuous drift audits, automated offsite disaster recovery, and strict secrets isolation.
## What I Built
Backup schedule: four systemd timers run a daily backup, a daily offsite copy, a weekly check that the offsite copy still opens, and an hourly check for changes; a separate hourly job snapshots agent memory.
Encrypted backups: each backup is encrypted with AES-256 before it leaves the server, then copied to Backblaze B2 cloud storage and mirrored to a private GitHub repository.
Disaster Recovery Runbook: Scripted restore procedure capable of bootstrapping the full multi-agent environment from bare Ubuntu 24.04.
Secrets Handling: Sensitive API tokens and credentials live in locked-down environment files and origin-bound vaults. Agents are set up so credentials are filled by the vault and never passed in conversation.
## Egress and anonymity
Web research that needs anonymity goes out through rotating egress over Tor and Cloudflare WARP, so no single route carries it and a failing route is dropped automatically.
Load balancer: a small proxy (glider) spreads requests across five Tor routes, and a second pool prefers Cloudflare WARP and falls back to Tor when WARP is slow or down.
Health checks: Glider checks every route every 30 seconds and drops a route after 2 failed checks, so traffic keeps flowing over the routes that still work.
Scope: This covers only the research and scraping traffic that is routed through it. It changes which route a request takes, nothing else.
Encrypted offsite backups: backups are encrypted, copied to cloud storage and a private GitHub repository, and a weekly job downloads one and checks it still opens.
## Outcome
A written restore script, and a weekly check that the latest offsite backup downloads and opens. Hourly checks for unexpected setting changes.
## Stack
systemd · OpenSSL · rclone · Backblaze B2 · GitHub · Bash · Python · Linux


# Finance ledger agent
Source: https://krishnendu.me/work/finance/

## Finance ledger agent: deterministic receipt normalization into Firefly III
Automated personal financial transaction normalization from read-only Gmail ingestion into self-hosted Firefly III using deterministic HTML and regex parsers.
Private personal finance tooling. Architecture and verification logic shown; zero amounts or merchant names disclosed.
Ingestion
Read-Only Gmail API (OAuth 2.0 PKCE)
Parsing Architecture
Rule-based parsers for each receipt format
Target Ledger
Self-Hosted Firefly III (REST API)
Idempotency
Order ID duplicate check · Automatic refund netting
## Problem
Manual expense tracking across multiple payment apps and email receipts is tedious and prone to double-counting. Receipts arrive with varying HTML layouts, complex tax splits, adjustments, and delayed refund notifications.
## What I Built
Read-only import: A Python job runs every six hours, reads my Gmail with read-only access, and picks out receipt emails.
Rule-based parsers: One parser per receipt format pulls out the amount, date and order number, so no AI model guesses at the numbers.
No duplicates: Each entry is tagged with its order number, and if the same email is read again the existing entry is found and skipped. Refunds are matched to the original order number and netted off.
Firefly III Integration: Staged transactions are posted to a self-hosted Firefly III instance via its authenticated REST API.
## Outcome
Receipts reach the ledger without me entering them by hand, and re-reading an email does not create a second entry.
## Stack
Python · Firefly III API · Gmail API · SQLite · scheduled jobs


# LinkedIn studio
Source: https://krishnendu.me/work/linkedin-studio/

## Personal LinkedIn studio: local drafting engine with anti-AI quality filter
A local drafting tool running on the socials agent that checks technical posts against voice notes and anti-AI writing patterns. Every post is reviewed and published manually.
Agent
socials agent
Filter Rules
34 known AI writing patterns · My written voice guide
Publishing Invariant
Mandatory Human Publishing (Zero Automated API Posting)
## Problem
AI-generated social media drafts often sound inflated, formulaic, and hollow, relying on buzzwords, long dashes and roundabout phrasing. Automated posting tools risk publishing unvetted claims without human editorial oversight.
## What I Built
Drafting app: A small Python web app on my server where I write, revise and file post ideas.
Voice guide: A written profile of how I write, built from my own past posts, that every draft is checked against.
Anti-AI Humanizer Gate: Scans drafts against 34 verified AI writing tells (eliminating dramatic fragmentation, promotional fluff, vague attributions, and forced metaphors).
Human Publishing Gate: The studio contains zero LinkedIn API credentials and cannot publish to the web. Completed drafts are copied and published manually.
## Outcome
Consistent personal technical voice, no automated filler, and human editorial control before publication. I check the facts in each post against my own project files before I publish.
## Limits
The system does not manage followers, schedule posts, or automate engagement; it is strictly a local composition and quality control tool.
## Stack
Python · Markdown · systemd · Linux

## List price vs subscription
At published list prices this volume comes to about $3,575.31 USD: $1,764.30 for proxied calls as computed by the proxy, and $1,811.01 as estimated by my runtime for direct Claude calls. I did not pay that figure. The direct Claude calls run on a flat subscription. I do not publish my bill, so read the list price as the honest upper bound and the subscription as the reason a personal system at this volume is affordable.
## Why the cache rate matters
An agent resends its system prompt, its tools and the conversation so far on every call. Without a prompt cache, every one of those tokens is read fresh at full price and full latency. A hit rate near 88.8% means almost all of that context was served from a stored prefix. It is the single number that decides whether a long running agent is affordable, and it is a design outcome, not luck: stable prompt prefixes, tool definitions that do not change between calls, and context that grows by appending rather than rewriting.
## What this tells you
The system is in daily use. The grid has no long gaps; this is not a demo run once for a screenshot.
Most tokens are context, not writing. Less than one token in a hundred is generated. That is what a tool using agent looks like: it reads a lot, decides, acts, and says little.
I pick models by cost and fit, not by brand. Cheap fast models carry the volume; expensive models get the judgement calls. The family table shows the ratio.
The numbers are reproducible. Every figure on this page comes from one JSON file rebuilt six hourly from the proxy database, my runtime's state database and the CLI transcripts, with the formulas in the note below. The file is public at /work/usage/data.json .
## How I count
This ledger counts only traffic through my proxy; the typed decision layer runs on its own service and is reported on Fast decisions .
Four categories, each token counted once: fresh input, cached read, cache write, output. Reasoning tokens are a subset of output and are shown only as "of which". Total is the sum of the four.
Proxy calls (OpenAI style): fresh input is prompt tokens minus cached tokens, cached read is cached tokens, output is completion tokens. This API does not report cache writes or reasoning, so those read n/r.
Direct calls (Anthropic style): fresh input is input tokens, cached read is cache read tokens, cache write is cache creation tokens, output is output tokens, and reasoning is reported separately inside output.
Claude Code: the same Anthropic style fields read from the transcript files, with duplicate message ids removed.
Cache hit rate is cached read divided by all input, where all input is fresh plus cached read plus cache write. Model names are grouped into families. List prices are the per token prices published by each provider as applied by the proxy or estimated by my runtime; they are not invoices. The window starts on 2026-09-13, the first day any source logged tokens.
## Accounting invariants and verification
The numbers on this page are computed deterministically during every site build. The build script queries the live databases and asserts twelve mathematical invariants before outputting static HTML:
Exact integer sum parity: The four components (fresh input, cache read, cache creation, output) sum exactly to the grand total across every source, model family, and daily record.
Zero double counting: Hermes direct Claude accounting includes only direct subscription rows, excluding proxy routes to prevent double counting.
Contiguous date continuity: The daily calendar grid contains zero missing dates between the tracking start date and today.
Non-negative fresh input: Every proxy daily record satisfies prompt tokens ≥ cached tokens, guaranteeing non-negative fresh input.
Reasoning containment: Reasoning tokens are strictly contained within output tokens on every reporting provider.
Telemetry capability reporting: Providers that do not report cache creation or reasoning are explicitly flagged with False capabilities rather than zero.
Family classification exhaustiveness: Every encountered model is mapped to a named family without version strings or unclassified fallbacks.
Calendar day alignment: All timestamps from 9router, Hermes, and Claude Code are normalized to Asia/Kolkata (IST) calendar boundaries.
Single partial day: Exactly one daily record (today) is flagged as partial.
Reproducible data artifact: The complete token dataset is published as machine-readable JSON at /work/usage/data.json .
Cost estimation boundaries: Dollar figures represent published list prices rather than subscription invoices.
Number refresh stability: The page template is static and values are injected deterministically to ensure automated refreshes change digits only.
Local probe: Run python3 scripts/gen_metrics.py to recompute metrics.json directly from 9router, Hermes state.db, and Claude Code transcripts.

# Projects
Source: https://krishnendu.me/projects/

## Machine learning and analytics projects
Every project is evaluated on the metric that genuinely reflects its objective: F1-Macro for severe class imbalance, MAP@3 for candidate ranking, and validation F1 for customer retention. High accuracy on lopsided data can flatter a model, so I lead with the score that shows how it does on the rare cases.
## Featured projects
## Smart MCQ solver (LoRA fine-tuning)
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of DeBERTa-v3 and RoBERTa using LoRA adapters for 5-option multiple-choice ranking. Blended in a 70:30 ensemble achieving 0.74242 MAP@3 on 500 unseen questions.
0.74242 MAP@3
## Comment classification
Feature engineering over 198,000 comments across four imbalanced label classes. Engineered 10,000+ n-grams, screened tabular features with chi-square and Kruskal-Wallis, and tuned LightGBM with Optuna (0.8202), then blended 3 models to reach 0.8293 F1-Macro.
0.8293 F1-MACRO
## Customer exit prediction
I compared 8 classifiers on 90,000 customer records from a financial institution, where few customers leave. I filled missing values, then tuned a Random Forest to a validation F1 of 0.6365 (accuracy 0.8414).
0.6365 F1
## VC deal analytics dashboard
Power BI deal analytics dashboard built on a 50,000-row synthetic star schema. Engineered 7 DAX measures and configured 2 AI visuals (Key Influencers and Decomposition Tree) for valuation driver ranking.
POWER BI · STAR SCHEMA
## More projects, in brief
## Virtual AI Teaching Assistant (RAG Pipeline)
Built a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) assistant using OpenAI embeddings and SQLite vector store. I split course materials into chunks and retrieved top-k relevant context via cosine similarity with FastAPI endpoints.
2025 · RAG · FASTAPI
## HR Attrition Dashboard (Power BI)
A two-page Power BI dashboard with 12 DAX measures on staff turnover, comparing hires with the same quarter before.
2026 · POWER BI · DAX
## Consumer Spend Segmentation (K-means++)
I grouped 62 survey respondents into 5 segments by monthly spend on personal care and fast food, using K-means++ (silhouette 0.540). Adding more spend categories and age made the segments less distinct, so I kept two.
2024 · K-MEANS++ · PYTHON
## Migration Determinants Regression Study (R)
Specified a 5-regressor OLS model in R across 28 Indian states analyzing out-migration. Found per-capita income (p=0.002), poverty (p=0.025), and unemployment (p=0.018) statistically significant at 5%.
2025 · R · OLS REGRESSION
## Influencer and Sponsor Matching Platform (Flask)
Full-stack web application connecting content creators and commercial sponsors using Flask, SQLite, and Jinja2 with 10+ analytical tracking dashboards and role-based access controls.
2024 · FLASK · FULL-STACK


# Research
Source: https://krishnendu.me/research/

## Research
Two research papers: one paper accepted for publication in Springer Nature conference proceedings (FICTA 2026) on spotting rare emotions in student chatbot conversations, and one systematic literature review on generative AI in marketing presented at the 10th Pan-IIM World Management Conference.
ORCID: 0009-0006-1176-1106
## Multi-Class Affect Detection in Educational Chatbots: Evidence from Imbalanced Dialogue Data
Accepted for publication in Springer Nature proceedings, Smart Innovation, Systems and Technologies series (Scopus indexed) · FICTA 2026
## Context and Problem
Educational dialogues contain severe class imbalance. Critical emotional states like confusion and frustration indicate when a learner is struggling, but they appear far less frequently than neutral or positive acknowledgments. Conventional classification algorithms optimize for overall accuracy, which allows them to score well while failing to detect the minority emotional states where pedagogical intervention is most needed.
## Methodology
I paired RoBERTa, a pretrained language model, with SVMSMOTE, a method that creates extra examples of the rare emotion classes so the model sees enough of them. I judged the models by how many of the rare Confused cases they caught (recall), not by overall accuracy.
## Key Findings
The proposed RoBERTa plus SVMSMOTE architecture achieved a 74.19% recall on the rare Confused emotion class, compared to less than 52% recall for baseline architectures without synthetic oversampling.
Venue
Springer Nature (FICTA 2026)
Primary Metric
74.19% Rare-Class Recall
Architecture
RoBERTa + SVMSMOTE
## Adoption and Implications of Generative AI in Marketing: A Systematic Review and Research Agenda
Presented at the 10th Pan-IIM World Management Conference 2025 · IIM Ranchi
## Context and Objective
Enterprise interest in generative AI for marketing automation has grown rapidly, but academic literature remained fragmented across practitioner whitepapers and narrow technical benchmarks. The review pulls together what published studies say about how companies use generative AI in marketing.
## Review Protocol
Following the PRISMA review method, I reviewed 29 Scopus articles published from 2020 to 2025 across technology readiness, consumer adoption, and regulatory considerations.
## Synthesis and Proposed Agenda
The review synthesised research priorities across algorithmic transparency in personalized marketing, consumer trust in synthetic media, workflow hand-offs between marketers and generative models, and data governance for automated campaigns.
Venue
10th Pan-IIM World Management Conference (WMC 2025)
Method
PRISMA Systematic Literature Review
Corpus
29 Scopus-Indexed Articles (2020 to 2025)
Focus
Generative AI in marketing
